Lower Bounds for Stochastic First-Order Algorithms with Variance Reduction in Nonconvex–Concave Minimax Optimization Thanks: This work was supported by the National Key R&D Program of China (Grant Nos. 2025YFA1017801 and 2025YFA1017800) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 12471294).

Jiayi Song1  Zi Xu1 1Department of Mathematics, College of Sciences, Shanghai University, Shanghai 200444, China ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: xuzi@shu.edu.cn.
Abstract

We establish complexity lower bounds for stochastic first-order algorithms in nonconvex–concave minimax optimization, allowing algorithms to use variance reduction. Our main contribution is a lower bound for a zero-respecting algorithm class that permits variance reduction, extending beyond the algorithmic restrictions imposed by some existing lower bounds. We consider objectives with an LL-Lipschitz continuous joint gradient, a compact convex dual domain of Euclidean radius at most DYD_{Y}, and a primal value function, defined by maximizing the objective over the dual variable, with initial suboptimality at most Δ\Delta. The target accuracy ε\varepsilon is measured by the gradient norm of the Moreau envelope of the constrained primal value function with parameter 1/(2​L)1/(2L). Under an unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with variance at most σ2\sigma^{2} and mean-square smoothness, we prove the lower bound Ω⁡(L2​DY​Δ​ε−3+L3​DY2​Δ​σ2​ε−6)\Omega\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta\varepsilon^{-3}+L^{3}D_{Y}^{2}\Delta\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-6}\right). This result quantifies the dependence on accuracy, dual-domain radius, and oracle noise even when variance reduction is allowed. We also establish complementary lower bounds for nonconvex–strongly-concave minimax optimization. With dual strong-concavity parameter μ>0\mu>0 and condition number κ:=L/μ\kappa:=L/\mu, we obtain Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ε−2+L​Δ​κ​σ2​ε−4)\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+L\Delta\kappa\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-4}\right) under the bounded-variance oracle model. Under the additional mean-square smoothness condition with constant L¯\bar{L}, we obtain Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ε−2+Δ​L¯​σ​κ3/2​ε−3)\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+\Delta\bar{L}\sigma\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}\right). Together, these results identify complexity barriers across the concave and strongly concave regimes, with the main nonconvex–concave bound remaining valid for algorithms that use variance reduction.

1 Introduction

Minimax optimization provides a natural framework for robust learning, adversarial training, and related problems in which a decision is optimized against a worst-case response [9, 10]. We study the stochastic first-order oracle complexity of problems of the form

minx∈X⁡Φ⁡(x),Φ⁡(x):=maxy∈Y⁡F⁡(x,y),\min_{x\in X}\Phi(x),\qquad\Phi(x):=\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y),

where X⊆ℝnX\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is closed and convex, Y⊆ℝpY\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} is compact and convex, and FF is jointly smooth. Our main focus is the nonconvex–concave (NC–C) setting, in which FF may be nonconvex in xx and is concave in yy. We also consider the nonconvex–strongly-concave (NC–SC) setting as a complementary regime. Strong concavity guarantees a unique dual maximizer and a differentiable primal value function, whereas the NC–C value function may be nonsmooth. We therefore measure stationarity through the Moreau envelope of the constrained primal value function.

Existing research has established first-order upper and lower bounds for both minimax regimes. In particular, deterministic NC–C optimization has an 𝒪⁡(ε−3)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}) complexity dependence, while stochastic methods attain an 𝒪⁡(ε−6)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-6}) dependence under bounded variance and mean-square smoothness [14, 13, 8, 16]. However, some existing stochastic lower bounds restrict oracle access in ways that exclude variance reduction. They therefore do not directly resolve whether the same complexity barrier persists for algorithms allowed to use coupled gradient evaluations with a shared random sample. This distinction matters because variance reduction improves the stochastic accuracy dependence in single-level nonconvex optimization [1, 4].

Our central goal is to establish lower bounds for stochastic first-order NC–C minimax optimization when variance reduction is allowed. We construct a mean-square-smooth stochastic oracle and prove a lower bound for zero-respecting algorithms that permits the same-sample queries used by variance-reduction methods. The result retains the 𝒪⁡(ε−6)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-6}) stochastic dependence, extending the scope of existing lower bounds rather than introducing a new accuracy exponent. We also develop complementary NC–SC lower bounds under bounded variance and mean-square smoothness, using a common chain-based construction.

1.1 Related work

Nonconvex optimization.

Carmon et al. [2, 3] developed zero-chain constructions and established the deterministic first-order lower bound Ω⁡(L​Δ​ε−2)\Omega(L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}) under an LL-Lipschitz gradient and an initial function-value gap bounded by Δ\Delta. For stochastic first-order oracles, Arjevani et al. [1] established Ω⁡(L​Δ​ε−2+L​Δ​σ2​ε−4)\Omega(L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}+L\Delta\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-4}) under bounded variance, where σ2\sigma^{2} bounds the oracle variance. Under mean-square smoothness with constant L¯\bar{L}, they obtained Ω⁡(Δ​L¯​σ​ε−3+(Δ​L¯+σ2)​ε−2)\Omega(\Delta\bar{L}\sigma\varepsilon^{-3}+(\Delta\bar{L}+\sigma^{2})\varepsilon^{-2}). This matches the accuracy dependence of recursive variance-reduction methods such as SPIDER [4]. Their oracle model also permits the same-sample gradient evaluations considered here, but their single-level hard instances do not capture primal–dual interactions.

Nonconvex–concave minimax optimization.

Under Moreau-envelope stationarity, Wu et al. [14] established the deterministic lower bound Ω⁡(L2​DY​Δ​ε−3)\Omega(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta\varepsilon^{-3}) and the bounded-variance stochastic lower bound Ω⁡(L3​DY2​Δ​σ2​ε−6)\Omega(L^{3}D_{Y}^{2}\Delta\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-6}), where DYD_{Y} bounds the dual-domain radius. Pan et al. [13] obtained the same deterministic ε−3\varepsilon^{-3} order under their normalization. Pan and Li [12] considered a different inner structure satisfying a Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition.

On the upper-bound side, deterministic first-order methods achieve essentially O~​(L2​DY​Δ​ε−3)\widetilde{O}(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta\varepsilon^{-3}) complexity [8]. In the stochastic setting, SAPD+ and SPDE achieve O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) oracle complexity under bounded variance, while VR-SPDE achieves O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) under mean-square smoothness [16]. These results motivate a lower bound that explicitly allows variance reduction. Our main result supplies such a bound: it preserves the 𝒪⁡(ε−6)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-6}) stochastic barrier under mean-square smoothness for a zero-respecting algorithm class with same-sample oracle access.

Nonconvex–strongly-concave minimax optimization.

Let κ:=L/μ\kappa:=L/\mu, where μ\mu is the dual strong-concavity parameter. Li et al. [7] established the deterministic lower bound Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ε−2)\Omega(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}) for zero-respecting first-order algorithms and the bounded-variance stochastic lower bound Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ε−2+L​Δ​κ1/3​σ2​ε−4)\Omega(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+L\Delta\kappa^{1/3}\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-4}). Zhang et al. [17] studied related deterministic and finite-sum bounds using a different construction and oracle formulation. More recently, Zhang et al. [18] established Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​σ2​ε−4)\Omega(L\Delta\kappa\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-4}) under bounded variance and Ω⁡(L¯​Δ​σ​κ¯3/2​ε−3)\Omega(\bar{L}\Delta\sigma\bar{\kappa}^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) under mean-square smoothness, with κ¯\bar{\kappa} denoting the condition parameter used in their formulation. Their hard instances use a quadratic lifting of a single-level nonconvex zero-chain.

On the upper-bound side, Lin et al. [8] established O~​(L​Δ​κ​ε−2)\widetilde{O}(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}) deterministic complexity. SPDE and VR-SPDE achieve O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) stochastic oracle complexity, respectively [16]. Our NC–SC results complement existing lower bounds through a product-weighted chain that also underlies our main NC–C construction. Under the same stationarity criterion and stochastic oracle conventions, the stochastic terms have the same κ\kappa and ε\varepsilon dependences as the corresponding upper bounds.

1.2 Main results and contributions

Our main contribution is an NC–C lower bound for stochastic first-order algorithms that are allowed to use variance reduction. The NC–SC results provide complementary bounds and demonstrate how a common construction applies to both minimax regimes.

  1. (i)

    An NC–C lower bound allowing variance reduction. We establish Ω⁡(L2​DY​Δ​ε−3+L3​DY2​Δ​σ2​ε−6)\Omega(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta\varepsilon^{-3}+L^{3}D_{Y}^{2}\Delta\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-6}) for zero-respecting algorithms under an unbiased, bounded-variance, mean-square-smooth oracle; see Theorem 4.8. The algorithm class permits same-sample queries and therefore allows variance reduction. We realize a smooth nonconvex zero-chain as the value function of a concave minimax problem with a bounded dual domain. A dual path delays coordinate revelation, while a Bernoulli gate preserves this delay and the value function under mean-square smoothness. The resulting stochastic lower bound has the same 𝒪⁡(ε−6)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-6}) dependence as VR-SPDE [16].

  2. (ii)

    A complementary bounded-variance NC–SC lower bound. We establish Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ε−2+L​Δ​κ​σ2​ε−4)\Omega(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+L\Delta\kappa\sigma^{2}\varepsilon^{-4}); see Theorem 6.5. A quadratic strongly-concave dual lift produces the deterministic propagation term, and a clipped stochastic dual potential hides the next block with positive probability, yielding the stochastic term.

  3. (iii)

    A complementary mean-square-smooth NC–SC lower bound. We establish Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ε−2+Δ​L¯​σ​κ3/2​ε−3)\Omega(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+\Delta\bar{L}\sigma\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}); see Theorem 7.6. We retain the delayed strongly-concave chain and replace the clipped noise potential by a smooth stochastic potential whose sample gradients satisfy both bounded variance and mean-square smoothness. These NC–SC results complement recent work rather than claim priority for this regime.

Notation, definitions, and assumptions.

The norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle are Euclidean. For a differentiable vector-valued map GG, ∇G\nabla G denotes its Jacobian, so ∇G(u)⊤v\nabla G(u)^{\top}v is the gradient of ⟨G⁡(u),v⟩\langle G(u),v\rangle. A function is C1,1C^{1,1} if it is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient. The notation OO and Ω\Omega suppresses constant factors, while O~\widetilde{O} additionally suppresses logarithmic factors.

For our problem classes, LL is the joint gradient Lipschitz constant, DYD_{Y} bounds the dual-domain radius, and Δ\Delta bounds the initial value-function gap: maxy∈Y⁡‖y‖≤DY\max_{y\in Y}\|y\|\leq D_{Y} and Φ⁡(0)−infx∈XΦ⁡(x)≤Δ\Phi(0)-\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x)\leq\Delta, with 0∈X0\in X. In the NC–SC setting, μ>0\mu>0 is the dual strong-concavity parameter and κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu. Let Φ¯:=Φ+ιX\overline{\Phi}:=\Phi+\iota_{X}, where ιX\iota_{X} is zero on XX and +∞+\infty outside XX. Its Moreau envelope with parameter λ>0\lambda>0 is Φ¯λ​(z):=infu∈X{Φ⁡(u)+‖u−z‖2/(2​λ)}\overline{\Phi}_{\lambda}(z):=\inf_{u\in X}\{\Phi(u)+\|u-z\|^{2}/(2\lambda)\}. We use SOS​(z):=‖∇Φ¯1/(2​L)​(z)‖S_{\rm OS}(z):=\|\nabla\overline{\Phi}_{1/(2L)}(z)\| and require a random output z^\widehat{z} to satisfy 𝔼⁡[SOS​(z^)2]≤ε2\mathbb{E}[S_{\rm OS}(\widehat{z})^{2}]\leq\varepsilon^{2}. This criterion applies to both minimax regimes, including nonsmooth value functions.

For a joint query point z=(x,y)z=(x,y) and random sample ω\omega, the oracle returns G⁡(z,ω)G(z;\omega) satisfying 𝔼ω​[G⁡(z,ω)]=∇F​(z)\mathbb{E}_{\omega}[G(z;\omega)]=\nabla F(z) and 𝔼ω​‖G⁡(z,ω)−∇F​(z)‖2≤σ2\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\|G(z;\omega)-\nabla F(z)\|^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}. Under mean-square smoothness, it also satisfies 𝔼ω​‖G⁡(z,ω)−G⁡(z′,ω)‖2≤L¯2​‖z−z′‖2\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\|G(z;\omega)-G(z^{\prime};\omega)\|^{2}\leq\bar{L}^{2}\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2}, with the same sample used at both points. Zero-respecting algorithms cannot activate coordinates before they are revealed by oracle responses, but our mean-square-smooth model permits same-sample queries. Formal definitions and parameter conditions are given in Section 2 and the corresponding theorems.

Organization.

Section 2 defines the function classes, stationarity criteria, and oracle models. Section 3 develops the common smooth chain. Section 4 proves the NC–C result. Section 5 constructs the deterministic delayed chain for NC–SC problems, and Sections 6 and 7 establish the corresponding bounded-variance and mean-square-smooth lower bounds. Section 8 concludes the paper.

2 Problem setup

We specify the function classes, the stationarity criteria, the zero-respecting algorithm classes, and the coordinate revelation framework used in the proofs.

2.1 Function classes and stationarity measures

For a differentiable objective F:X×Y→ℝF:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}, let

Φ⁡(x):=maxy∈Y⁡F⁡(x,y),x∈X.\Phi(x):=\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y),\qquad x\in X.

No convexity is required in the primal variable.

Definition 2.1 (Nonconvex–(strongly)concave function class).

Given L>0L>0, μ≥0\mu\geq 0, Δ>0\Delta>0, and D>0D>0, let ℱNC​-​μ​C​(L,μ,Δ,D)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{NC}\text{-}\mu\mathrm{C}}(L,\mu,\Delta,D) denote the class of continuously differentiable objectives F:X×Y→ℝF:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}, over all finite dimensions, satisfying:

  1. (i)

    X⊆ℝdxX\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} and Y⊆ℝdyY\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} are nonempty closed convex sets containing zero, and

    diam⁡(Y)≤D.\operatorname{diam}(Y)\leq D.
  2. (ii)

    FF is jointly LL-smooth:

    ‖∇F​(z)−∇F​(z′)‖≤L​‖z−z′‖,z,z′∈X×Y.\|\nabla F(z)-\nabla F(z^{\prime})\|\leq L\|z-z^{\prime}\|,\qquad z,z^{\prime}\in X\times Y.
  3. (iii)

    For every x∈Xx\in X, the function F⁡(x,⋅)F(x,\cdot) is concave on YY.

  4. (iv)

    The primal value function

    Φ⁡(x):=maxy∈Y⁡F⁡(x,y)\Phi(x):=\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y)

    satisfies

    Φ⁡(0)−infx∈XΦ⁡(x)≤Δ.\Phi(0)-\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x)\leq\Delta.
  5. (v)

    For every x∈Xx\in X and y,y′∈Yy,y^{\prime}\in Y,

    F⁡(x,y′)≤F⁡(x,y)+⟨∇yF​(x,y),y′−y⟩−μ2​‖y′−y‖2.F(x,y^{\prime})\leq F(x,y)+\langle\nabla_{y}F(x,y),y^{\prime}-y\rangle-\frac{\mu}{2}\|y^{\prime}-y\|^{2}.

Strong concavity bounds F⁡(x,⋅)F(x,\cdot) ensures existence and uniqueness of its maximizer y∗​(x)y^{*}(x) on the closed set YY. The value function is differentiable and satisfies

∇Φ​(x)=∇xF​(x,y∗​(x)).\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_{x}F(x,y^{*}(x)).

For the NC–C class, define the extended value function ϕ:=Φ+ιX\phi:=\Phi+\iota_{X}. For 0<λ<L−10<\lambda<L^{-1}, its proximal point and Moreau envelope are

pλ​(x)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(x) :=arg​minw∈X⁡{Φ⁡(w)+12​λ​‖w−x‖2},\displaystyle:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{w\in X}\left\{\Phi(w)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|w-x\|^{2}\right\}, (2.1)
ϕλ​(x)\displaystyle\phi_{\lambda}(x) :=minw∈X⁡{Φ⁡(w)+12​λ​‖w−x‖2}.\displaystyle:=\min_{w\in X}\left\{\Phi(w)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|w-x\|^{2}\right\}.

The envelope is continuously differentiable, with

∇ϕλ​(x)=λ−1​(x−pλ​(x)).\nabla\phi_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-p_{\lambda}(x)).
Definition 2.2 (Zero-respecting first-order algorithm).

Let (𝒙0,𝒚0)=(0,0)(\boldsymbol{x}^{0},\boldsymbol{y}^{0})=(0,0). For every t≥0t\geq 0, let

𝒮xt:=⋃i=0t(supp⁡(𝒙i)∪supp⁡(𝒈xi)),𝒮yt:=⋃i=0t(supp⁡(𝒚i)∪supp⁡(𝒈yi)),\mathcal{S}_{x}^{t}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{t}\left(\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{x}^{i})\cup\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{g}_{x}^{i})\right),\qquad\mathcal{S}_{y}^{t}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{t}\left(\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{y}^{i})\cup\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{g}_{y}^{i})\right),

where (𝒈xi,𝒈yi)(\boldsymbol{g}_{x}^{i},\boldsymbol{g}_{y}^{i}) is the gradient response returned by the oracle at the ii-th query. A first-order algorithm is called zero-respecting if every feasible iterate (𝒙t+1,𝒚t+1)∈X×Y(\boldsymbol{x}^{t+1},\boldsymbol{y}^{t+1})\in X\times Y satisfies

supp⁡(𝒙t+1)⊆𝒮xt,supp⁡(𝒚t+1)⊆𝒮yt.\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{x}^{t+1})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{x}^{t},\qquad\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{y}^{t+1})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{y}^{t}.

2.2 Oracle and algorithm classes

Definition 2.3 (Stochastic first-order oracle).

The stochastic first-order oracle of a differentiable function f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} returns

𝒪fsfo​(x,y)=(f⁡(x,y),∇^x​f​(x,y,ξ),∇^y​f​(x,y,ξ)),(x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴,\mathcal{O}_{f}^{\text{sfo}}(x,y)=(f(x,y),\widehat{\nabla}_{x}f(x,y;\xi),\widehat{\nabla}_{y}f(x,y;\xi)),\qquad(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

where ξ\xi is a random variable satisfying

𝔼ξ​[∇^​f​(x,y,ξ)]=∇f​(x,y),𝔼ξ​[‖∇^​f​(x,y,ξ)−∇f​(x,y)‖2]≤σ2.\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\widehat{\nabla}f(x,y;\xi)]=\nabla f(x,y),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}f(x,y;\xi)-\nabla f(x,y)\|^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}.

Under the mean-square smoothness (MSS) assumption, we additionally require

𝔼ξ​[‖∇^​f​(x,y,ξ)−∇^​f​(x′,y′,ξ)‖2]≤L¯2​‖(x,y)−(x′,y′)‖2,(x,y),(x′,y′)∈𝒳×𝒴,\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\!\left[\left\|\widehat{\nabla}f(x,y;\xi)-\widehat{\nabla}f(x^{\prime},y^{\prime};\xi)\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\bar{L}^{2}\left\|(x,y)-(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\right\|^{2},\qquad(x,y),(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

where the same random variable ξ\xi is used at both query points.

Definition 2.4 (Zero-respecting first-order algorithm).

Let (𝒙0,𝒚0)=(0,0)(\boldsymbol{x}^{0},\boldsymbol{y}^{0})=(0,0). For every t≥0t\geq 0, let

𝒮xt:=⋃i=0t(supp⁡(𝒙i)∪supp⁡(𝒈xi)),𝒮yt:=⋃i=0t(supp⁡(𝒚i)∪supp⁡(𝒈yi)),\mathcal{S}_{x}^{t}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{t}\left(\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{x}^{i})\cup\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{g}_{x}^{i})\right),\qquad\mathcal{S}_{y}^{t}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{t}\left(\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{y}^{i})\cup\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{g}_{y}^{i})\right),

where (𝒈xi,𝒈yi)(\boldsymbol{g}_{x}^{i},\boldsymbol{g}_{y}^{i}) is the gradient response returned by the oracle at the ii-th query. A first-order algorithm is called zero-respecting if every feasible iterate (𝒙t+1,𝒚t+1)∈X×Y(\boldsymbol{x}^{t+1},\boldsymbol{y}^{t+1})\in X\times Y satisfies

supp⁡(𝒙t+1)⊆𝒮xt,supp⁡(𝒚t+1)⊆𝒮yt.\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{x}^{t+1})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{x}^{t},\qquad\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{y}^{t+1})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{y}^{t}.

2.3 Zero-chain framework

For u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and θ≥0\theta\geq 0, define

progθ⁡(u):=max⁡({j∈[d]:|uj|>θ}∪{0}).\operatorname{prog}_{\theta}(u):=\max\bigl(\{j\in[d]:|u_{j}|>\theta\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).

In particular, prog0⁡(u)\operatorname{prog}_{0}(u) is the largest index in the support of uu.

Definition 2.5 (First-order zero-chain).

For z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define

prog0⁡(z):=max⁡({j∈[d]:zj≠0}∪{0}).\operatorname{prog}_{0}(z):=\max\bigl(\{j\in[d]:z_{j}\neq 0\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).

A differentiable function F:ℝd→ℝF:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is a first-order zero-chain if, for every z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

prog0⁡(∇F​(z))≤min⁡{prog0⁡(z)+1,d}.\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\nabla F(z))\leq\min\{\operatorname{prog}_{0}(z)+1,d\}.
Definition 2.6 (Probability-pp zero-chain).

Let p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], and let f:𝒳⊆ℝd→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a differentiable function equipped with a stochastic first-order oracle 𝒪fsfo​(𝒙)=(f⁡(𝒙),∇^​f​(𝒙,ξ))\mathcal{O}_{f}^{\text{sfo}}(\boldsymbol{x})=(f(\boldsymbol{x}),\widehat{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x};\xi)). We call ff a probability-pp zero-chain with respect to this oracle if, for every 𝒙∈𝒳\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X} with r:=prog0​(𝒙)<dr:=\text{prog}_{0}(\boldsymbol{x})<d,

ℙξ​(prog0​(∇^​f​(𝒙,ξ))=r+1)≤p,ℙξ​(prog0​(∇^​f​(𝒙,ξ))>r+1)=0.\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\left(\text{prog}_{0}(\widehat{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x};\xi))=r+1\right)\leq p,\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\left(\text{prog}_{0}(\widehat{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x};\xi))>r+1\right)=0.

Here, the probability is taken over the randomness of the oracle.

3 Common hard-instance components

We construct a common zero-chain φm:ℝm→ℝ\varphi_{m}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} whose smoothness, unfinished-chain gradient barrier, and initial gap are uniform in the dimension:

4 The NC–C lower bound under mean-square smoothness

We realize the common chain as the value function of a concave saddle problem. A long dual path gives the deterministic term, while a Bernoulli-gated four-node path gives the stochastic term under mean-square smoothness.

When ω=1\omega=1, the tridiagonal edge term can reveal at most the next coordinate in the full order (4.8).

This sequence has length MM. The support argument in Lemma 4.2 prevents any of its coordinates from being skipped. Every new coordinate in this sequence requires a successful draw, and a single call reveals at most one of them: all points in that batch were selected from the previously revealed support before the common draw. Revealing the terminal primal coordinate therefore requires at least MM successful draws. The same conclusion applies to a transcript-derived output by Definition 2.4.

Theorem 6.5 (Bounded-variance lower bound).

There are absolute constants κ0,cBV,cacc>0\kappa_{0},c_{\rm BV},c_{\rm acc}>0 such that the following holds. Fix L,μ,Δ>0L,\mu,\Delta>0 and write κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu. For κ≥κ0\kappa\geq\kappa_{0}, σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, and 0<ε≤cacc​L​Δ0<\varepsilon\leq c_{\rm acc}\sqrt{L\Delta}, there is one fixed instance and oracle in the NC–SC bounded-variance class for which every zero-respecting first-order algorithm using at most

N≤cBV​(L​Δ​κε2+L​Δ​κ​σ2ε4)N\leq c_{\rm BV}\left(\frac{L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{L\Delta\kappa\sigma^{2}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\right)

oracle calls satisfies 𝔼​‖∇Φ​(x^)‖>ε\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat{x})\|>\varepsilon.

Proof.

Set

κ0\displaystyle\kappa_{0} =max{2,32Ld},cacc=min{cb10240​C∗,cd10240​Ld},\displaystyle=\max\{2,32L_{\rm d}\},\qquad c_{\rm acc}=\min\left\{\frac{c_{b}}{\sqrt{10240C_{*}}},\frac{c_{d}}{\sqrt{10240L_{\rm d}}}\right\},
cBV\displaystyle c_{\rm BV} =12​min⁡{cdet,cbv}.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min\{c_{\rm det},c_{\rm bv}\}.

Let

A=L​Δ​κε2,B=L​Δ​κ​σ2ε4.A=\frac{L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}}{\varepsilon^{2}},\qquad B=\frac{L\Delta\kappa\sigma^{2}}{\varepsilon^{4}}.

Proposition 5.3 gives a fixed deterministic instance with hardness threshold

Td=cdet​A.T_{\rm d}=c_{\rm det}A.

Its exact-gradient oracle has variance zero and therefore satisfies the bounded-variance condition for every prescribed σ≥0\sigma\geq 0. The residual bound holds pathwise, so it also holds in expectation for randomized zero-respecting algorithms.

Lemma 6.3 and Proposition 6.4 give a second fixed instance for which every budget satisfying

N≤cbv​(L​Δε2+B)N\leq c_{\rm bv}\left(\frac{L\Delta}{\varepsilon^{2}}+B\right)

has

𝔼​‖∇Φ​(x^)‖≥8​ε.\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat{x})\|\geq 8\varepsilon.

In particular, this instance is hard up to the threshold

Ts=cbv​B.T_{\rm s}=c_{\rm bv}B.

Choose the deterministic instance when Td≥TsT_{\rm d}\geq T_{\rm s} and the stochastic instance otherwise. This selection depends only on L,Δ,κ,σ,εL,\Delta,\kappa,\sigma,\varepsilon. Furthermore,

max⁡{Td,Ts}=max⁡{cdet​A,cbv​B}≥12​min​{cdet,cbv}​(A+B)=cBV​(A+B).{\max\{T_{\rm d},T_{\rm s}\}=\max\{c_{\rm det}A,c_{\rm bv}B\}\geq\frac{1}{2}\min\{c_{\rm det},c_{\rm bv}\}(A+B)=c_{\rm BV}(A+B).}

Thus the budget in the theorem does not exceed the hardness threshold of the selected fixed instance. Proposition 5.3 gives residual at least 16​ε16\varepsilon in the deterministic case, while Lemma 6.3 gives expected residual at least 8​ε8\varepsilon in the stochastic case. In either case the expected residual is strictly larger than ε\varepsilon, which proves the claim. ∎

7 The mean-square-smooth NC–SC lower bound

We next impose mean-square smoothness in addition to bounded variance and gate the common chain through a shared Bernoulli sample.

Remark 7.7.

When σ=0\sigma=0, Proposition 5.3 and Lemma 7.5 give the deterministic Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ/ε2)\Omega(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}/\varepsilon^{2}) lower bound under the deterministic accuracy condition alone. The positive-σ\sigma range (7.3) is used only for the Bernoulli-gated construction.

8 Conclusion

This work establishes complexity barriers for stochastic first-order minimax optimization, with a primary focus on NC–C problems when variance reduction is allowed. Our main result shows that the ε−6\varepsilon^{-6} stochastic barrier persists under mean-square smoothness for zero-respecting randomized algorithms with same-sample oracle access. Its significance lies not in a new accuracy exponent, but in extending the lower bound to an algorithm class that permits variance reduction. The complementary NC–SC results capture the dependence on accuracy and conditioning under bounded variance and mean-square smoothness.

The common product-weighted chain separates the difficulty of attaining value-function stationarity from the delay in revealing primal–dual information. This separation enables hard instances across different concavity and stochastic regularity regimes, while preserving the coupled oracle access used by variance-reduction methods. Together, the results show that stronger stochastic regularity does not by itself guarantee an improved minimax accuracy dependence: the interaction between primal and dual variables remains a fundamental source of difficulty within the algorithm class considered here.

An important next step is to determine whether these barriers extend beyond zero-respecting algorithms. Resolving this question would clarify the extent to which the observed complexity is intrinsic to stochastic minimax optimization rather than tied to coordinate-revelation restrictions.

A.3 Proof of Lemma 3.3

Proof.

The separable term has no coordinates beyond rr. For every j>rj>r, we have uj=0u_{j}=0, and therefore

∂jHm​(u)=−4​S′​(0)+J′​(0)=0.\partial_{j}H_{m}(u)=-4S^{\prime}(0)+J^{\prime}(0)=0.

Hence ∇Hm​(u)\nabla H_{m}(u) is supported on the first rr coordinates.

For the coupling term, define

qi​(u)=Pi−1​(u)2​(1−S⁡(ui))2​𝒦​(ui),Qm​(u)=∑i=1mqi​(u).q_{i}(u)=P_{i-1}(u)^{2}(1-S(u_{i}))^{2}\mathcal{K}(u_{i}),\qquad Q_{m}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}q_{i}(u).

Fix j>r+1j>r+1. We prove ∂jqi​(u)=0\partial_{j}q_{i}(u)=0 for every ii. If i<ji<j, then qiq_{i} depends only on u1,…,uiu_{1},\ldots,u_{i}, so it is independent of uju_{j}. If i=ji=j, then Pj−1P_{j-1} contains the factor S⁡(ur+1)=S⁡(0)=0S(u_{r+1})=S(0)=0, while Pj−1P_{j-1} is independent of uju_{j}. Thus both qj​(u)q_{j}(u) and ∂jqj​(u)\partial_{j}q_{j}(u) vanish. Finally, if i>ji>j, then Pi−1P_{i-1} contains both S⁡(ur+1)S(u_{r+1}) and S⁡(uj)S(u_{j}). Differentiation with respect to uju_{j} may replace the latter by S′​(uj)S^{\prime}(u_{j}), but the distinct factor S⁡(ur+1)=0S(u_{r+1})=0 remains. Hence ∂jqi​(u)=0\partial_{j}q_{i}(u)=0 also in this case. Summing over ii gives

∂jQm​(u)=0,j>r+1.\partial_{j}Q_{m}(u)=0,\qquad j>r+1.

Therefore ∇Qm​(u)\nabla Q_{m}(u), and hence ∇φm​(u)=∇Hm​(u)+∇Qm​(u)\nabla\varphi_{m}(u)=\nabla H_{m}(u)+\nabla Q_{m}(u), has no nonzero component after coordinate r+1r+1. B.1 Proof of Lemma 4.1

Proof.

(τn+(n−1)−1−(n−1)−1−(n−1)−1τn+(n−1)−1).\begin{pmatrix}\tau_{n}+(n-1)^{-1}&-(n-1)^{-1}\\ -(n-1)^{-1}&\tau_{n}+(n-1)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.

Substituting τn=1/[2​(n−1)]\tau_{n}=1/[2(n-1)] and inverting this matrix proves (4.3); the same calculation applies when n=2n=2, in which case there are no interior coordinates.

Positive definiteness gives a unique maximizer, whose first-order equation is

Bn​vi=ϑn​Wi​(u)​(e1−γ⁡(ui)​en).B_{n}v^{i}=\vartheta_{n}W_{i}(u)\bigl(e_{1}-\gamma(u_{i})e_{n}\bigr).

ϑn2​Wi​(u)22​(e1−γ⁡(ui)​en)𝖳​Bn−1​(e1−γ⁡(ui)​en)=Wi​(u)2​𝒦​(ui).\frac{\vartheta_{n}^{2}W_{i}(u)^{2}}{2}(e_{1}-\gamma(u_{i})e_{n})^{\mathsf{T}}B_{n}^{-1}(e_{1}-\gamma(u_{i})e_{n})=W_{i}(u)^{2}\mathcal{K}(u_{i}).

Summing over the blocks gives (4.5).

The vectors Bn−1​e1B_{n}^{-1}e_{1} and Bn−1​enB_{n}^{-1}e_{n} interpolate linearly between their endpoint values in (4.3). Every entry therefore lies between zero and 6​(n−1)/56(n-1)/5. Since |γ|≤1/2|\gamma|\leq 1/2,

‖vi,∗​(u)‖∞≤2​n​Wi​(u),‖vi,∗​(u)‖≤2​n​Wi​(u).\|v^{i,*}(u)\|_{\infty}\leq 2\sqrt{n}\,W_{i}(u),\qquad\|v^{i,*}(u)\|\leq 2nW_{i}(u).

The bounds Wi≥0W_{i}\geq 0 and ∑iWi2≤1\sum_{i}W_{i}^{2}\leq 1 then establish (4.6). ∎

B.2 Proof of Lemma 4.2

Proof.

The dual Hessian is −diag⁡(Bn,…,Bn)-\operatorname{diag}(B_{n},\ldots,B_{n}), and ‖Bn‖op≤5\|B_{n}\|_{\rm op}\leq 5. This proves concavity and the required bound for the dual Hessian block.

To bound the remaining blocks, write Ti​(u)=Wi​(u)​γ​(ui)T_{i}(u)=W_{i}(u)\gamma(u_{i}). The directional derivative estimates in the proof of Lemma 3.1 give

∑i|∇Wi​(u)​[h]|≤CW​‖h‖,∑i|∇2Wi​(u)​[h,h]|≤DW​‖h‖2.\sum_{i}|\nabla W_{i}(u)[h]|\leq C_{W}\|h\|,\qquad\sum_{i}|\nabla^{2}W_{i}(u)[h,h]|\leq D_{W}\|h\|^{2}.

The product rule, together with |γ|≤1/2|\gamma|\leq 1/2, |γ′|≤1/4|\gamma^{\prime}|\leq 1/4, |γ′′|≤1/8|\gamma^{\prime\prime}|\leq 1/8, and ∑iWi≤1\sum_{i}W_{i}\leq 1, yields

∑i|∇Ti​(u)​[h]|\displaystyle\sum_{i}|\nabla T_{i}(u)[h]| ≤(CW2+14)​‖h‖,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{C_{W}}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\right)\|h\|,
∑i|∇2Ti​(u)​[h,h]|\displaystyle\sum_{i}|\nabla^{2}T_{i}(u)[h,h]| ≤(DW2+CW2+18)​‖h‖2.\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{D_{W}}{2}+\frac{C_{W}}{2}+\frac{1}{8}\right)\|h\|^{2}.

On 𝒴m,n\mathcal{Y}_{m,n}, both ϑn​|v1i|\vartheta_{n}|v_{1}^{i}| and ϑn​|vni|\vartheta_{n}|v_{n}^{i}| are at most two. When n=4n=4 and ‖v‖≤8\|v\|\leq 8, they are at most 8/68/\sqrt{6}. Pairing the second directional estimates with these bounded endpoint coefficients gives a dimension-free bound for the primal Hessian block. The first directional estimates and ϑn≤1/2\vartheta_{n}\leq 1/\sqrt{2} give a dimension-free bound for the mixed block. Together with the bound for ∇2Hm\nabla^{2}H_{m}, these estimates prove joint smoothness on both domains after fixing a sufficiently large universal CcC_{\rm c}. We also require Cc≥CφC_{\rm c}\geq C_{\varphi} for the later value-function estimates. All second-derivative bounds hold almost everywhere and extend to global gradient bounds because the first derivatives are continuous.

For the support statement, a dual gradient block has the form

∇vi𝒟m,n=−Bn​vi+ϑn​Wi​(u)​(e1−γ⁡(ui)​en).\nabla_{v^{i}}\mathcal{D}_{m,n}=-B_{n}v^{i}+\vartheta_{n}W_{i}(u)\bigl(e_{1}-\gamma(u_{i})e_{n}\bigr).

The tridiagonal term can expose only the next dual coordinate. Before uiu_{i} is revealed, ui=0u_{i}=0, so the source at the last dual coordinate vanishes because γ⁡(0)=0\gamma(0)=0. At such a point, the contribution to the new primal component is

∂ui𝒟m,n=−ϑn​Wi​(u)​γ′​(0)​vni.\partial_{u_{i}}\mathcal{D}_{m,n}=-\vartheta_{n}W_{i}(u)\gamma^{\prime}(0)v_{n}^{i}.

Here HmH_{m} and ∂iWi\partial_{i}W_{i} contribute zero because S′​(0)=J′​(0)=0S^{\prime}(0)=J^{\prime}(0)=0, while all later dual blocks are zero. Thus uiu_{i} cannot appear before vniv_{n}^{i}. Finally, every later source contains the factor S⁡(ui)=S⁡(0)=0S(u_{i})=S(0)=0; its derivative at an unrevealed primal coordinate also vanishes because S′​(0)=0S^{\prime}(0)=0. These observations cover each possible location of the frontier in (4.8) and establish the zero-chain property. ∎

Appendix C Proofs for the deterministic NC–SC chain

C.1 Proof of Lemma 5.1

Proof.

We next verify the coordinate order. Consider a query supported on a prefix of the displayed order. Before any coordinate of that block is revealed, its source term can expose only y1iy_{1}^{i}. The gradient of hh is ℓ\ell-Lipschitz.

Thus the certified joint gradient Lipschitz constant of FF is

L^MSS:=ℓ+c⁡(1+a2)≤μ+L2≤5​L8<L.\widehat{L}_{\rm MSS}:=\ell+c(1+a^{2})\leq\mu+\frac{L}{2}\leq\frac{5L}{8}<L.

For the sample gradient, embed g⁡(y,ω)g(y;\omega) in the full primal–dual space and apply the triangle inequality in L2​(Ω,ℝ2​m)L^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{2m}). Its joint mean-square Lipschitz constant is at most L¯/4+c⁡(1+a2)≤3​L¯/4≤L¯\bar{L}/4+c(1+a^{2})\leq 3\bar{L}/4\leq\bar{L}, proving (7.6).

Finally, we bound the initial gap. Lemma 3.2 gives φm​(0)−infφm≤5​m\varphi_{m}(0)-\inf\varphi_{m}\leq 5m, so h⁡(0)−infh≤5​δ​λ​m≤Δ/2h(0)-\inf h\leq 5\delta\lambda m\leq\Delta/2. The descent lemma for the lower-bounded ℓ\ell-smooth function hh gives ‖∇h​(0)‖2≤2​ℓ​(h⁡(0)−infh)\|\nabla h(0)\|^{2}\leq 2\ell(h(0)-\inf h). For any yy,

h⁡(y)−c2​‖y‖2≤h⁡(0)+⟨∇h​(0),y⟩−c−ℓ2​‖y‖2.h(y)-\frac{c}{2}\|y\|^{2}\leq h(0)+\langle\nabla h(0),y\rangle-\frac{c-\ell}{2}\|y\|^{2}.

Maximizing this upper bound gives Φ⁡(0)≤h⁡(0)+‖∇h​(0)‖2/[2​(c−ℓ)]\Phi(0)\leq h(0)+\|\nabla h(0)\|^{2}/[2(c-\ell)]. Conversely, evaluating the inner problem at y=a​xy=ax gives Φ⁡(x)≥h⁡(a​x)\Phi(x)\geq h(ax), so infxΦ⁡(x)≥infh\inf_{x}\Phi(x)\geq\inf h. Combining these inequalities yields

Φ⁡(0)−infxΦ⁡(x)≤cc−ℓ​(h⁡(0)−infh)≤2⋅Δ2=Δ.\Phi(0)-\inf_{x}\Phi(x)\leq\frac{c}{c-\ell}(h(0)-\inf h)\leq 2\cdot\frac{\Delta}{2}=\Delta.

∎

E.2 Proof of Lemma 7.5

Proof.

Let FdF_{\rm d} be the deterministic instance from Proposition 5.3. Equip it with the constant-sample representation

fd​(z,ω):=Fd​(z)for every sample ​ω.f_{\rm d}(z;\omega):=F_{\rm d}(z)\qquad\text{for every sample }\omega.

Then, for every zz,

𝔼ω∇fd(z;ω)=∇Fd(z).\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\nabla f_{\rm d}(z;\omega)=\nabla F_{\rm d}(z). (E.1)

Consequently,

𝔼ω​‖∇fd​(z,ω)−∇Fd​(z)‖2=0≤σ2.\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\|\nabla f_{\rm d}(z;\omega)-\nabla F_{\rm d}(z)\|^{2}=0\leq\sigma^{2}. (E.2)

For any z,z′z,z^{\prime}, the LL-smoothness in Proposition 5.3 and L¯≥L\bar{L}\geq L give

𝔼ω​‖∇fd​(z,ω)−∇fd​(z′,ω)‖2≤L¯2​‖z−z′‖2.\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\|\nabla f_{\rm d}(z;\omega)-\nabla f_{\rm d}(z^{\prime};\omega)\|^{2}\leq\bar{L}^{2}\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2}. (E.3)

Proposition 5.3 also gives

Fd​(x,⋅)​ is ​μ​-strongly concave,Φd​(0)−infxΦd​(x)≤Δ.F_{\rm d}(x,\cdot)\text{ is }\mu\text{-strongly concave},\qquad\Phi_{\rm d}(0)-\inf_{x}\Phi_{\rm d}(x)\leq\Delta.

Equations (E.1)–(E.3) verify the remaining stochastic-oracle requirements. Hence (Fd,fd)(F_{\rm d},f_{\rm d}) belongs to the same mean-square-smooth class. ∎
